extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting newspaper news stories using the standard (inverted) structure, lead-writing, sentence/paragraph construction, and practical reporting techniques (speech notes, outlines, space constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard news structure (lead, catch-all, elaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard structure contains three parts: (1) the introduction or 'lead'; (2) the catch-all or bric-a-brac division; and (3) the elaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead compresses the whole story into one or two paragraphs; the catch-all gathers odds-and-ends (minor mentions) and should follow the lead; the elaboration expands the lead's items in order. Use this structure to present concentrated information quickly while reserving space for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead built on the six questions (Who, What, Where, When, Why, How)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead is built upon six questions: 'Who?' 'What?' 'Where?' 'When?' 'Why?' 'How?'. When these 'five W V' have been answered, the story is outlined and nothing remains to be given except details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compress essential facts into one or two paragraphs so a reader can decide quickly whether to read further. Example: 'The city council (Who) abolished all-night parking (What), by an 8 to 2 vote (How) last night (When) at a special meeting (Where) at which action was recommended by the traffic committee (Why).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a secondary lead for important but secondary aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: If other aspects, though secondary, are of high interest, summarize them in a 'secondary lead' (additional paragraph) rather than overloading the top lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the top-facet lead first, then a secondary paragraph briefly summarizing other principal actions; expand these later in the elaboration in the same order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination lead and numbered/statistical lead for multi-item stories
rubrics_metrics.description: When one story contains several principal actions, a combination lead (single paragraph covering multiple items) or a numbered list (statistical form) can present information coherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbered lists improve clarity for multiple items and are valuable despite some editors' hostility; one-facet lead followed by a numbered list often satisfies both clarity and editorial tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of the catch-all (put it after the lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: The catch-all (minor-mention bracket) gathers various odds and ends and should follow the lead rather than be placed at the very end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing the catch-all after the lead protects it from being cut by make-up editors who frequently drop the last paragraph; in small/medium cities omitting the catch-all can anger readers who expect local mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaboration must expand lead items in the order presented
rubrics_metrics.description: After the skeleton (lead and secondary), flesh out the story by expanding the lead: present details impossible to crowd into the first paragraph and expand secondary-lead items in the same order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep order consistent to preserve coherence (e.g., expand item 1, then 2, etc.). Use quotations and specifics to give life to elaborations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted emphasis (strongest material first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because newspapers are read hastily, the climax is at the start and the end contains weaker material: the strongest facet first at sentence, paragraph, and story level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invert conventional literary order: put the most important fact up front and hold lesser details until the end of sentences/paragraphs so skimming readers acquire essentials from openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invert sentence order to place the important fact first
rubrics_metrics.description: Form sentences so the main fact comes at the start rather than at the end (e.g., put what the post voted at the top of the sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example transformation: 'At the meeting of John W. Allen post...it was voted unanimously...' becomes 'The American Legion state convention will be invited to meet in this city next year, John W. Allen post voted unanimously at its meeting last night at Memorial Hall,...' — place the vote first, secondary details later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific rather than general statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer concrete, specific information to generic, vague phrasing (e.g., avoid 'A special display'—pin down what, who, and how many).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific sentences are more interesting and allow individual headlines; test an opening sentence by whether a 'once only' headline can be written from it. Example: 'A display of water colors by nine of the city's high school students is on view this week...' is better than a general statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test openings by whether a unique headline can be written
rubrics_metrics.description: A good test of the quality of an opening sentence is whether a 'once only' headline can be written from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot write a headline that fits only that story (and not a dozen others), the opening sentence is likely deficient and too general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix sentence lengths and grammatical patterns (change of pace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a variety of sentence lengths and grammatical constructions to obtain tone and avoid monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, jerky sentences for vivid fast action; longer flowing sentences for leisurely observations. Mix several short, one long, several short, etc., and employ as many grammatical variations as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep paragraphs short for narrow newspaper columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Because newspaper columns are narrow (averaging about two inches) and type small, paragraphs must be short to remain legible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normal paragraph need not run more than six typed lines; long paragraphs become unwelcome in narrow columns and hurt readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to the prescribed space (learn to fit the column)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must learn to write to space: editors may say 'Half a column' and expect copy to fit that precise length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train to produce the correct amount of material for a given space; inability to do so can be professionally costly. Practice tightening or expanding copy to meet space requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preplan/outlining ('write it on the wall')
rubrics_metrics.description: Good reporters plan a story mentally or by outlining during the event—'write it on the wall'—so that the actual typing is merely transcription of pre-arranged structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask questions while observing (How big is the story? What will readers wish to know? Is it news or entertainment?) Make an outline: choose the lead, secondary lead items, and order of expansions; use outlining until it becomes mental habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-line feature (spark within first six words)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'first-line feature' is a sparkling bit jammed into the first six words based on a factual observation that reinforces a thin story without departing from standard structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The feature must arise from observation/fact-gathering (not mere word-wrenching). Examples: 'Five goldfish were killed and one man was slightly bruised when...' or mentioning the sleeping dog in a house-fire story to attract reader attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overcrowding the lead sentence (Verboten #1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overload the lead sentence with too many details; the five W's (and V) are all a lead can cram in without exploding—minor details must be held until later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of bad practice: an extremely long single sentence listing name, age, address, parent occupation, how the raft was built, distance from shore, water depth measurement, etc.; these details are all good but not for the lead sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid complicated, rambling sentences (Verboten #2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rambling, complicated sentences usually indicate inadequate thinking and produce paragraphs too long for narrow newspaper columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cure by distinguishing important lead information from minor details; keep sentences concise so paragraphs remain within acceptable length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't open sentences with unimportant explanatory words/time (Verboten #3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid openings like 'At 8 o'clock tonight, at the high-school auditorium...' which delay the main action until the end of the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such periodic, inverted sentences make the reader wait and are signs of immature writing; lead with the important fact instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't begin with generalities like 'plans for' or 'work is progressing' (Verboten #4)
rubrics_metrics.description: General, vague openings fail to tell the reader what is actually happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pin down the story: tell what the plans are, how much work is done, or what the meeting will do rather than using generic lead-ins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid opening with vague crowd figures (Verboten #5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginnings such as 'A crowd of 27,500...' mean little because most readers cannot visualize such numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find a concrete, visual detail to convey the crowd's size or significance rather than relying on unimpressive figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't open with blurbs like 'presence of mind saved the life' (Verboten #6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague blurbs fail to convey what actually happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how the 'presence of mind' was manifested and what the quick thinker did, rather than using the abstract phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't waste principal verbs on subordinate-clause actions (Verboten #7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sentences that allocate main verb emphasis to minor or subordinate actions, which misplaces emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad example: 'Although he swam to shore, Burke's teeth chattered from the cold.' The syntax suggests the drowning is incidental; restructure to place the important fact where it belongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid starting sentences repeatedly with the same word or letter (Verboten #8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A succession of sentences beginning with 'The...' becomes monotonous and killingly dull.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain variety by changing syntax and sentence openings; vary structures to keep reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning sentences with 'there is'/'there are' (Verboten #9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'there is' and 'there are' are backhanded, indirect, and sleepy when placed at the top of a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use more direct, active constructions at the top of sentences to keep prose vigorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline and lead must be strong because readers skim
rubrics_metrics.description: Many readers glance at headlines and top paragraphs only; if the headline is well written, readers may extract all they need from it and not read the full story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write headlines and leads that carry the essential facts and stand alone when necessary; don't rely on readers to go beyond the top of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech reporting: emphasize direct quotes and accurate reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Good speech reports aim to reflect a speaker's 6,500 words accurately within 200 words, largely by direct quotes rather than paraphrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech reporting is exacting and provides chances to show individuality and thoroughness. Strive to capture effective direct quotations and reflect the speaker's tone and content accurately in the short report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking notes and shorthand/abbreviations for reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should develop a compact note system: abbreviations and symbols can substitute for formal shorthand; mastery of a simplified shorthand helps but is not always necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reuse college-note abbreviations or create new ones (e.g., 'R' for Republicans); build 150–200 symbols for speed. Short, sensible abbreviations allow accurate reporting without full stenographic training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the story mentally before typing ('write it on the wall')
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter plans and experiments with phrasing and structure while attending the event so that actual typing is merely transferring the pre-arranged story from mind to page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask planning questions during coverage (How big is it? What will readers wish to know? Is it news or entertainment?). Mental outlining shortens desk time and improves first-draft quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train to write correctly on first draft under deadline pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Although reporters sometimes revise once, they must generally 'write correctly the first time' because deadlines limit revision opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the habit of producing accurate, clear copy under time pressure; don't use 'pressure' as an excuse for weak writing—train to produce your best regardless of mood or time.
